strengths: Clear and compelling empirical motivation: the paper visualizes (Fig. 1, 3, 6) a measurable gap between when a token becomes a stable top-1 prediction and when it is actually committed by threshold-based parallel decoders, which grounds the proposed method in an observed phenomenon rather than pure intuition.

The proposed Trace Credit mechanism is simple, training-free, and easy to integrate (a log-domain additive prior derived from an exponentially decayed, focused accumulation of past logits), making it plausible as a practical, low-cost addition to existing dLLM inference pipelines.

Broad empirical validation: results are reported on eight benchmarks spanning reasoning, coding, QA, and knowledge tasks, using two different backbones (LLaDA-8B-Instruct and LLaDA-MoE-Instruct), which strengthens generalizability claims within the LLaDA model family.

Extensive supporting analyses are provided, including hyperparameter ablations (alpha, beta), block-length ablations, scalability tests up to 4K generation length, and a full-distribution variant (CD*) that trades some speed for robustness, giving a reasonably complete picture of the method's behavior.

Thorough orthogonality experiments combining CreditDecoding with KV-cache variants, early stopping, PyTorch compilation, and FP8 quantization (Table 3, 4) demonstrate that gains are largely additive with existing system- and algorithm-level optimizations, valuable for practical adoption.

Reasonable reproducibility support: pseudocode (Algorithm 1), fixed hyperparameters, use of public model weights and standardized evaluation (OpenCompass) with a hardware/implementation-agnostic metric (TPF).
weaknesses: No direct empirical comparison against other closely related 'history-aware' decoding methods explicitly cited in Related Work (e.g., Wang et al. 2025 'Time is a feature,' which also exploits temporal/historical dynamics in dLLM decoding, or PC-Sampler, path-planning, DPaD). Without such comparisons, it is hard to assess whether Trace Credit offers a genuine advance over prior history-exploiting approaches rather than a re-parameterization of similar ideas.

Mixed results on several benchmarks (e.g., DROP, LCB, GSM8K show small negative deltas in Table 1) are acknowledged but not deeply analyzed; the paper attributes GSM8K degradation to 'minor fluctuations' without a rigorous account of when/why the method can hurt accuracy, weakening the soundness of the overall efficiency-accuracy trade-off claim.

Generalization is only demonstrated within one model family (LLaDA and its MoE variant); no results on architecturally distinct dLLMs (e.g., Dream, SEED-diffusion) are shown despite these being discussed in Related Work, limiting confidence that the phenomenon and fix generalize broadly across dLLM designs.

The core Trace Credit formulation (global decay plus focused top-1 enhancement, log-domain fusion) is motivated heuristically via empirical curves rather than derived from a principled probabilistic argument; the choice of beta, gamma, alpha and their interactions are tuned empirically per setting without theoretical justification, and gamma is fixed without ablation or explanation of its selection.

TPF (tokens-per-forward) is the primary efficiency metric in the main tables, but actual wall-clock throughput (TPS), which matters most for real deployment claims of 'speedup,' is relegated to the appendix and only reported for the orthogonality experiments, making the headline speedup numbers (e.g., 5.48x) somewhat less directly interpretable as real-world latency gains.

The paper's exposition is at times repetitive (the same 'redundant computation'/'history-agnostic' framing and analysis appear nearly verbatim in the introduction and methodology sections) and contains minor grammatical/formatting issues, which slightly hurts clarity and polish expected for camera-ready main-conference work.

No code/artifact release is mentioned explicitly, and while the method is simple enough to reimplement from the pseudocode, independent verification of exact reported numbers would still require careful re-implementation given the multiple interacting hyperparameters and per-dataset tuning.

strengths: The paper is grounded in a clear empirical motivation: Figures 1, 3, and 6 convincingly show a temporal gap between when a token's prediction stabilizes and when it is finally decoded under threshold-based parallel decoding, which is a useful diagnostic contribution independent of the proposed fix.
CreditDecoding is simple, training-free, and architecture-agnostic, requiring only a lightweight modification to the logit-fusion step, which lowers the barrier for adoption.

Evaluation spans eight benchmarks across knowledge, reasoning, code, and QA tasks, and is run on two different model scales/architectures (dense LLaDA-8B and LLaDA-MoE), which is a reasonably broad testbed.

The orthogonality experiments (Section 5.5, Appendix C.4) with KV cache, early stop, PyTorch compiler, and FP8 quantization are a valuable addition that tests compatibility with realistic deployment pipelines rather than only the vanilla baseline.

Ablations over the hyperparameters (α, β) and block length are provided, giving some insight into sensitivity, and the paper also proposes and evaluates a full-distribution variant (CD*) as an alternative operating point.
weaknesses: The headline '5.48× speedup' is measured in Tokens-Per-Forward (TPF), a proxy metric, not wall-clock throughput (TPS). Appendix Table 3 reveals that when CreditDecoding is combined with the strongest existing baseline (Fast-dLLM w/ KV cache), the actual TPS gain is only +31% (39.38 → 51.40) with a negligible accuracy gain (+0.12), even though the corresponding TPF gain is reported as +217%. This large TPF/TPS divergence suggests substantial per-step overhead from the credit computation that is not reflected in the headline numbers, and it materially undercuts the practical significance of the advertised speedup, which practitioners would realize primarily in the non-KV-cache, weaker-baseline regime.

Novelty is not clearly differentiated from directly related concurrent work. Wang et al. (2025, 'Time is a feature: Exploiting temporal dynamics in diffusion language models') is cited only briefly in related work despite tackling essentially the same problem (leveraging decoding history/temporal dynamics to improve dLLM decoding); the paper does not empirically or conceptually compare against this baseline, making it hard to assess the incremental contribution over the closest prior art.

The method introduces three hand-tuned hyperparameters (α, β, γ) with no principled derivation; the ablation (Fig. 7) shows performance is non-monotonic and dataset-dependent, and the paper explicitly notes 'optimal values vary by dataset,' raising concerns about robustness/generalization to unseen tasks and about how much of the reported gain depends on benchmark-specific tuning.

No stronger, more recent competing acceleration/planning baselines discussed in Related Work (e.g., SlowFast sampling, dLLM-cache, PC-Sampler, DPaD) are empirically compared against; the only quantitative comparison throughout is to Fast-dLLM, which weakens the evidentiary basis for claiming a state-of-the-art contribution.

Accuracy improvements are frequently marginal (often <1 point, sometimes negative, e.g., GSM8K -0.76, LCB -0.61 for LLaDA-8B) and no variance/multiple-seed results are reported, so it is unclear whether the reported gains are statistically distinguishable from noise.

Writing and presentation have notable rough edges: incomplete/garbled sentences (e.g., start of Section 5.1 'Implementation (Nie et al., 2025) and LLaDA-MoE-7B-A1B-Instruct...'), stray punctuation, and dense, hard-to-parse figures (Figs. 1, 3, 6) that are not self-contained without extensive cross-referencing to the text.

Scalability claims (Section 5.4) are based on only two long-length settings (1K, 4K) with block length fixed at 64, and the observed TPF speedup plateaus around 7× regardless of length, which somewhat undercuts the framing that CreditDecoding 'scales effectively' beyond what is already achievable by existing block-parallel decoding.

strengths: Clear and compelling empirical motivation: the decoding-boundary/rank analysis (Figures 1, 3, 6) convincingly demonstrates that many tokens reach top-1 confidence well before they are committed, providing a concrete, visualizable justification for the proposed mechanism.
The proposed Trace Credit / CreditDecoding method is simple, training-free, and easy to implement (clear formulation and pseudocode in Algorithm 1), which lowers the barrier to adoption.

Broad empirical coverage: two model families (dense LLaDA-8B and LLaDA-MoE), eight benchmarks spanning reasoning, coding, QA, and knowledge tasks, plus scalability tests up to 4K tokens and thorough hyperparameter/block-length ablations.

Orthogonality experiments with KV-cache, early stopping, PyTorch compiler, and FP8 quantization are a genuine practical strength, showing the method composes with existing inference optimizations and reporting both TPF and TPS in the appendix.
The TPF metric choice is well justified for reproducibility since it is hardware-agnostic, and the method requires no retraining or architecture change.
weaknesses: No direct experimental comparison against other closely related acceleration/history-aware methods discussed in Related Work (e.g., Wang et al. 2025 'Time is a Feature', PC-Sampler, path-planning, DPaD, SlowFast sampling); only Fast-dLLM and the vanilla baseline are benchmarked, making it hard to judge the method's relative standing against the current state of the art.

Reported accuracy gains are small and inconsistent: several benchmarks (DROP, LiveCodeBench, GSM8K, Math) show negative score deltas under CreditDecoding, which somewhat contradicts the claimed 'minimal or no accuracy loss' and the abstract's headline aggregate improvement; no variance/seed information or significance testing is provided to assess whether these small deltas are meaningful versus noise.

Hyperparameters (α, β) appear tuned per experiment and the paper acknowledges 'optimal values vary by dataset' (Section 5.3), yet a single global setting is used for the main results table without describing a held-out tuning protocol, raising concern about selection on test performance.

The mathematical form of the trace-credit update (decay factor, concave exponent γ, log-domain fusion) is motivated heuristically rather than derived from a principled objective; there is no theoretical analysis of when/why this improves both speed and accuracy simultaneously, nor bounds on error introduced by the credit prior.

Memory/compute overhead of maintaining a per-position, per-vocabulary credit tensor (L×|V|) is not discussed or quantified, which is relevant to the practicality claims given the method's aim of efficiency.

Generalization is limited to one model family (LLaDA and its MoE variant); no evaluation on other dLLM backbones (e.g., Dream) is provided despite these being discussed as representative systems, limiting confidence that the approach generalizes across architectures.

Minor inconsistencies in reported numbers (e.g., 4.10x vs 4.11x speedup for LLaDA-MoE) and some imprecise claims in the text (e.g., calling a −0.76 GSM8K drop 'minor fluctuations') slightly undermine rigor and clarity.

strengths: Identifies a concrete, well-motivated inefficiency in dLLM parallel decoding (early-but-unconfident predictions causing redundant remasking), supported by clear empirical visualizations (Figs. 3-5) and a theoretical derivation of the minimum logit gain needed for early decoding.

The proposed EMA-based 'trace credit' mechanism is simple, training-free, and easy to integrate as it only modifies logits without touching sampling/selection procedures, making it broadly compatible with other systems.

Extensive empirical validation: four dLLM architectures/scales (8B to 100B, dense and MoE, pure-diffusion and block-diffusion), eight benchmarks spanning knowledge/reasoning/coding, and multiple decoding schemes (threshold, Top-K, Top-K margin).
Thorough ablations covering hyperparameters (α, β, γ), block size, a full-distribution credit variant, and top-K focused-enhancement variants, which strengthen confidence in the design choices.

Demonstrated orthogonality with mainstream inference optimizations (KV cache, PyTorch compiler, FP8 quantization, early stop) with both TPF and end-to-end TPS measurements, supporting practical applicability.

Honest limitations and failure-mode analysis (e.g., degraded performance on reasoning-heavy tasks with strong causal dependencies), including plausible explanations tied to confidence-convergence stability.
Reasonably reproducible: public model weights, standardized OpenCompass evaluation, and use of a hardware-agnostic efficiency metric (TPF).
weaknesses: Accuracy gains are modest and inconsistent across benchmarks — several datasets (DROP, LCB, GSM8K, MATH on LLaDA-8B) show negative score deltas, which somewhat undercuts the abstract's framing of consistent improvement alongside speedup.
Results are reported as single runs without variance across seeds, making it hard to assess whether the small (often <1 point) score changes are statistically meaningful versus noise.

Core hyperparameters (α, β, γ) are tuned specifically on LLaDA-8B-Instruct and reused elsewhere; while a tuning-free adaptive variant is proposed, the paper acknowledges it does not always reach optimal performance and still may require per-task tuning in practice.
The method's weakness on reasoning-intensive tasks (math, complex code) is a significant practical limitation given these are common target use-cases for LLM acceleration research.

Novelty is somewhat incremental relative to existing temporal/historical-signal decoding work cited in the paper (e.g., Wang et al. 2025); the distinction between this prior work and the proposed EMA credit mechanism is not deeply analyzed or empirically contrasted.

Baseline comparisons are largely limited to Fast-dLLM; broader comparison against other recent dLLM acceleration/calibration methods mentioned in related work (e.g., path-planning remasking, PC-sampler) is missing, limiting the assessment of relative advantage.

strengths: Clear, well-motivated empirical observation (temporal consistency of target-token confidence trajectories) that provides an intuitive basis for the proposed mechanism.
The method itself is simple, training-free, and easy to integrate (modifies only logits), which is a practical virtue.
Broad empirical coverage: four dLLM architectures/scales (8B to 100B, dense and MoE, pure-diffusion and block-diffusion), eight benchmarks spanning knowledge, reasoning, and code.

Reasonably thorough ablation studies (hyperparameters α/β/γ, block size, top-K vs. full-distribution credit variants) and an orthogonality study showing compatibility with KV-cache, compiler, quantization, and early-stop.
A tuning-free adaptive schedule is proposed to reduce deployment overhead, improving practical usability.
Honest limitations and failure-mode section acknowledging degradation on reasoning-heavy tasks and dataset-dependent hyperparameters.
weaknesses: Novelty is not clearly established relative to closely related prior work that already exploits temporal/historical signals in dLLM decoding (e.g., Wang et al. 2025 'Time is a feature', dLLM-cache, SlowFast sampling), all cited but never directly compared empirically; the paper's central claim of being a new 'history-aware' mechanism needs a head-to-head comparison to substantiate its contribution over these works.

All main results are single-run (explicitly stated), with no variance/seed analysis, which is concerning given that many reported score deltas are extremely small (e.g., +0.13, -0.08, -0.24, 0.00) and could plausibly be within noise, undermining the robustness of the 'consistent improvement' claim.

The headline '+0.48 accuracy' and 'consistent improvement' framing masks substantial per-task variance: several benchmarks show score regressions (DROP, LCB, GSM8K on LLaDA-8B; DROP, KorBench on LLaDA-MoE), which weakens the generality claim stated in the abstract and conclusion.

The theoretical derivation (minimum logit gain, Eq. 4-5) is only loosely connected to the final heuristic EMA-based credit rule; the jump from the formal analysis to the specific update rule (Eq. 6) and its hyperparameters (β, γ) is motivated mostly by intuition rather than rigorous justification.

Hyperparameters (α=0.65, β=0.7, γ=0.2) are tuned specifically on LLaDA-8B-Instruct and then reused elsewhere; the paper itself admits optimal values are dataset/model-dependent, and the tuning-free variant does not always match the tuned version's trade-off, raising concerns about how much the reported gains depend on post-hoc tuning on the test-reported benchmarks.

Inconsistent experimental protocol between the headline figure (Figure 1, w/o Early Stop) and main tables (w/ Early Stop) could present an overly favorable visual impression of speedup without full transparency on how this choice affects comparability.

No clear statement of code/artifact release, which combined with single-run reporting and multiple tunable hyperparameters, raises mild reproducibility concerns despite otherwise detailed configuration descriptions.

The contribution, while practically useful, is incremental in nature (a logit-level EMA-based confidence calibration layered on top of existing threshold decoding), and the gains, when properly contextualized against prior temporal/historical methods, may not clearly constitute a significant enough advance for a strong main-conference claim.

strengths: Identifies and clearly analyzes a genuine and previously underexplored inefficiency in dLLM parallel decoding: tokens are often predicted correctly well before their confidence crosses the decoding threshold, causing redundant remasking iterations.

The proposed Trace Credit / CreditDecoding mechanism is training-free, simple to implement (operates purely on logits), and is shown to be compatible/orthogonal with a wide range of existing acceleration techniques (KV cache, compiler fusion, FP8 quantization, early stop, threshold decoding).

Broad empirical validation: experiments span 8 benchmarks across knowledge, reasoning, and coding, and multiple model families/scales (LLaDA-8B, LLaDA-MoE, SDAR, LLaDA2-Mini/Flash, 7B to 100B parameters), plus generation-length scaling (up to 4k tokens).

Thorough ablation and diagnostic analyses (hyperparameter sweeps for α/β/γ, block-size ablation, top-K vs full-distribution credit variants, decoding-boundary visualizations, TPS end-to-end measurements) that support the mechanistic claims with reasonable rigor.

Honest limitations/failure-mode section explaining and analyzing performance degradation on reasoning-heavy tasks (math, code), attributing it to causal dependency and unstable confidence convergence, which strengthens credibility.
A tuning-free adaptive variant is proposed to reduce deployment overhead, addressing a natural criticism of hyperparameter sensitivity.
weaknesses: All main results are single-run (explicitly stated), with many reported deltas being very small (e.g., ±0.05–0.5 points), making it difficult to assess whether reported improvements/degradations are statistically meaningful rather than noise.

Performance gains are inconsistent across benchmarks: several datasets (DROP, GSM8K, MATH, LCB) show slight accuracy degradation under the main method, undermining the headline claim of simultaneous universal speed and accuracy improvement.

The theoretical motivation (Eqs. 4–5 minimum logit gain derivation) is only loosely connected to the final EMA-based credit design; the transition from the derivation to the specific update rule (Eq. 6) and hyperparameterization (β, γ) is more heuristic/empirical than rigorously justified.

No direct empirical comparison against other temporal/historical-signal decoding methods cited in related work (e.g., Wang et al. 2025 'Time is a feature'), leaving the relative advantage of Trace Credit over existing history-aware approaches unclear.

Optimal hyperparameters (α, β, γ) are tuned per model/dataset, and the tuning-free variant does not consistently match the tuned version's performance-efficiency trade-off, somewhat weakening the 'training-free/practical' framing.

Reported headline speedup figures (e.g., 5.48×) depend on specific configuration choices (Early Stop enabled/disabled, block size, generation length), and the paper's own figures show substantially different speedup/accuracy trade-offs across settings, which could give a misleadingly strong headline impression.
